title: History: projectile vomiting in an infant (pyloric stenosis) and fluids

header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking

related.why: The other infant surgical emergency: intussusception

brief.scenario: Noah Whitfield, 6 weeks old, has been referred by his GP with vomiting. His mother, Emma, is with him.
brief.task: Take a focused history from Noah's mother. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to summarise, then asked about examination findings, blood results and preoperative management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Is the vomit bilious? Then how dry is he?
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating it as reflux, or rushing him to theatre before the alkalosis is corrected.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Introduce yourself, confirm Noah's details, and ask Emma to tell you what's been happening.

grid.label: Opening with the parent
grid.fail: Launches into questions without introduction or acknowledging her worry.
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms Noah's name and age and Emma's relationship; open question.
grid.high: Acknowledges her exhaustion and worry early and keeps plain language throughout.

grid.label: Characterising the vomiting (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Doesn't ask the colour of the vomit.
grid.pass: Onset, frequency, timing after feeds, force (projectile), colour: non-bilious; blood; hungry afterwards.
grid.high: States green vomit would mean malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise; asks about progression over the fortnight.

grid.label: Hydration and nutrition
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about wet nappies or weight.
grid.pass: Feed type and volume, wet nappies, stools, weight gain, alertness.
grid.high: Asks for the red-book weights and compares with birth weight; asks about lethargy as a red flag.

grid.label: Background and risk factors
grid.fail: Omits birth history and family history.
grid.pass: Gestation, birth weight, first child, family history of pyloric stenosis; other symptoms: fever, diarrhoea, jaundice.
grid.high: Links risk factors: boys affected four to five times as often; family history; preterm infants at higher risk of postoperative apnoea.

grid.label: Summary and diagnosis
grid.pass: Two weeks of non-bilious projectile vomiting, hungry baby, poor weight gain, fewer wet nappies: likely pyloric stenosis.
grid.high: Gives differentials (reflux, overfeeding, infection, malrotation if bilious) and states he is dehydrated.

grid.label: Examination and confirmation
grid.fail: Doesn't look for dehydration, or relies on the mass alone.
grid.pass: Dehydration signs; test feed for visible peristalsis and an olive in the right upper quadrant; ultrasound.
grid.high: Gives ultrasound criteria: muscle thickness 3 mm or more, channel length 15 mm or more.

grid.label: Electrolytes and paradoxical aciduria
grid.fail: Expects a metabolic acidosis, or cannot explain the urine.
grid.pass: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Aldosterone drives sodium reabsorption; as potassium runs out, hydrogen ions are excreted: acid urine.
grid.high: Orders a capillary gas with chloride and glucose; knows sodium may also be low.

grid.label: Fluids and timing (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Books theatre tonight before correcting the alkalosis, or gives hypotonic maintenance (NG29 advises isotonic).
grid.pass: NG tube, NBM. 10 ml/kg 0.9% saline only if shocked. Isotonic glucose-potassium fluid for maintenance plus deficit; NG losses as saline with potassium.
grid.high: States it is a medical, not surgical, emergency: pyloromyotomy only once chloride, bicarbonate and potassium are normal; electrolytes rechecked more often than daily while abnormal.

pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical doctors. Are you Noah's mum? Can I check his date of birth? Tell me what's been happening.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: When did it start, and how often? How soon after feeds? Is it forceful? What colour: milky, green or bloody? Is he hungry afterwards?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Noah, 6 weeks, has two weeks of non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds. He's hungry afterwards, has fewer wet nappies and hasn't gained weight. This is likely pyloric stenosis.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Dehydration: fontanelle, mucous membranes, capillary refill, heart rate. Then a test feed, looking for peristalsis and feeling for an olive in the right upper quadrant. Ultrasound confirms it.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Aldosterone reabsorbs sodium; with potassium depleted, hydrogen ions are excreted, so the urine is acid.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Nil by mouth and an NG tube. 10 ml/kg of 0.9% saline, 34 ml, only if shocked. Isotonic fluid with glucose and potassium for maintenance, about 14 ml/h, plus his deficit, and replace NG losses with 0.9% saline with potassium.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel. You must be exhausted with this; I'll ask some questions and then explain what I think.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Has it got more forceful over the two weeks? Has it ever been green? Green vomit would worry me about a twisted bowel.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Do you have his red book? What did he weigh at birth and at his last check? Has he been more sleepy than usual?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Did his dad have an operation on his stomach as a baby? That fits, and boys are affected four to five times as often.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Noah, 6 weeks, first child, term: two weeks of worsening non-bilious projectile vomiting, hungry after feeds, fewer wet nappies, below birth weight. Father had pyloromyotomy. Likely pyloric stenosis and he's dehydrated. Differentials include reflux, infection, and malrotation if bilious.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Muscle thickness 3 mm or more and channel length 15 mm or more.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A capillary gas with chloride and glucose, plus urea and electrolytes. The sodium may be low too.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: When can he go to theatre?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Pyloromyotomy isn't an emergency. Only once chloride is at least 100, bicarbonate below 30 and potassium normal, with electrolytes rechecked more often than daily while they're abnormal.

failures.move: Not asking whether the vomit is green.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: misses malrotation with volvulus, which can infarct the midgut within hours.

failures.move: Taking him to theatre before the alkalosis is corrected.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: metabolic alkalosis causes respiratory depression and postoperative apnoea, worsened by anaesthesia.
Misreads the gas and gives the wrong fluid.

failures.move: Relying on a palpable olive and skipping the hydration assessment.

recovery.when: You forgot the colour of the vomit
recovery.line: One important question: has the sick ever been green or yellow-green?

recovery.when: Asked a fluid rate you can't recall
recovery.line: I'd use Holliday-Segar maintenance, isotonic with glucose, and check electrolytes to guide changes.

knowledge.fact: Non-bilious projectile vomiting in a hungry infant; olive palpable on test feed.
Hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Boys four to five times more often.
Ultrasound: muscle 3 mm or more, length 15 mm or more.

Resuscitation bolus 10 ml/kg glucose-free isotonic crystalloid over under 10 minutes; maintenance 100 ml/kg/day for the first 10 kg, isotonic; ongoing losses with 0.9% saline containing potassium; electrolytes at least every 24 hours, more often while abnormal.
Abnormal electrolytes: chloride below 100 or bicarbonate 30 or more mmol/l.

recall.think: Bilious vomiting is volvulus until proven otherwise; dehydration and alkalosis.
recall.say: "Likely pyloric stenosis: resuscitate and correct before surgery."
do: Ask colour of vomit and wet nappies
Capillary gas with chloride and glucose
NG tube, isotonic fluids with potassium
recall.trap: Pyloromyotomy is not an emergency; the fluids are.

sources.name: NICE NG29: Intravenous fluid therapy in children and young people in hospital
sources.supports: Clinical dehydration and shock features (Table 1); resuscitation bolus 10 ml/kg glucose-free crystalloid with sodium 131-154 mmol/l over under 10 minutes (1.3.1); Holliday-Segar maintenance 100 ml/kg/day for first 10 kg (1.4.1); maintenance with isotonic crystalloids with 5% glucose (1.4.3), so not hypotonic fluids; replace ongoing losses with 0.9% sodium chloride containing potassium (1.5.3); electrolytes and glucose at least every 24 hours (1.2.4, 1.2.5)

sources.name: Craig R, Deeley A. Anaesthesia for pyloromyotomy. BJA Educ 2018;18:173-7
sources.supports: Boys affected four to five times as often as girls; hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; paradoxical aciduria as the kidney excretes hydrogen ions to conserve sodium and water; preterm infants at risk of postoperative apnoea, also reported in term infants after pyloromyotomy; metabolic alkalosis causes respiratory depression and apnoea, so it must be corrected before surgery; a medical, not surgical, emergency

sources.name: Iqbal CW, Rivard DC, Mortellaro VE, Sharp SW, St Peter SD. Evaluation of ultrasonographic parameters in the diagnosis of pyloric stenosis relative to patient age and size. J Pediatr Surg 2012;47:1542-7
sources.supports: Pyloric muscle thickness of 3 mm or more and length of 15 mm or more as accepted ultrasound criteria

sources.name: Dalton BG, Gonzalez KW, Boda SR, Thomas PG, Sherman AK, St Peter SD. Optimizing fluid resuscitation in hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. J Pediatr Surg 2016;51:1279-82
sources.supports: Abnormal electrolytes defined as chloride below 100 mmol/l or bicarbonate 30 mmol/l or more, used as the marker of resuscitation before anaesthesia

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Clinical features of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (non-bilious projectile vomiting, test feed, olive, visible peristalsis), risk factors, Ramstedt pyloromyotomy; bilious vomiting and malrotation with volvulus

partner.opening: Please take a focused history from Noah's mother. I'll stop you at 6 minutes to summarise.
partner.actorBrief: You are Emma Whitfield, 29, Noah's mother. Noah is your first baby. Opening line: "He keeps being sick after every feed. It shoots right out of him." Emotional state: tired, anxious, a little defensive because your sister says he's just a sicky baby and you worry it's your fault. Volunteer only the vomiting. Release other facts only when asked (see reveals). Hidden concern: that you've been feeding him wrongly; say so only if asked what worries you. Expectation: you want him sorted today. If told he needs an operation, ask if it's dangerous.

reveals.trigger: Asks when it started and how often
reveals.finding: Started two weeks ago, now after nearly every feed, getting worse.
"It shoots across the room." Milky, sometimes curdled. Never green, never blood.
"He screams for another feed straight away."
Formula, about 90 ml every 3 hours. Two wet nappies today, used to be 6-8. Stools small and infrequent.
Red book: 3.5 kg at birth, 3.9 kg at 4 weeks, 3.45 kg today. "He's sleepier today."

reveals.trigger: Asks about birth and family history
reveals.finding: Born at 39 weeks, normal delivery. First child. His father had an operation on his stomach as a baby.
Say: "Please stop there and summarise your history."

reveals.trigger: After the summary, candidate asks for examination findings
reveals.finding: Heart rate 170, capillary refill 3 seconds, sunken fontanelle, dry mouth, alert but quiet. On test feed: visible peristalsis left to right; olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant.
Capillary gas: pH 7.52, bicarbonate 34, chloride 88, potassium 2.9, sodium 132, glucose 4.1 mmol/l.

push.question: What would you look for on examination?
push.expect: Dehydration signs; test feed; peristalsis and olive; ultrasound.

push.question: Interpret these results.
push.expect: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; mild hyponatraemia.

push.question: Why is his urine acid?
push.expect: Volume depletion and aldosterone; with potassium depleted, hydrogen ions are excreted to reabsorb sodium.

push.question: How will you manage him before surgery?
push.expect: NG tube; bolus only if shocked; isotonic maintenance with glucose and potassium; replace NG losses; theatre when corrected.

curveballs.prompt: "Actually, this morning it was bright green."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Bilious vomiting: malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise; urgent senior review and upper GI contrast study.

curveballs.prompt: The anaesthetist is free now; can we do the pyloromyotomy tonight?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: correct the alkalosis and potassium first; pyloromyotomy is not an emergency.

curveballs.prompt: "Is it because I fed him wrong?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: the muscle at the stomach outlet has thickened; nothing she did caused it, and an operation fixes it.

curveballs.prompt: He becomes mottled with capillary refill of 5 seconds.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Hypovolaemic shock: 10 ml/kg (about 34 ml) 0.9% saline over under 10 minutes, reassess, repeat if needed, senior help.
